**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract

   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order

5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is

  specifies, `[]` if none. A point that only execution can settle is a
  finding marked needs-validation, with the exact JSON payload and command
  a human should run. A needs-validation finding's severity is that of what
  you have shown, by reading or by a test that passed, and `low` when you
  have shown nothing; its `summary` states the impact if it is confirmed.
* `coverage`: one entry per label of this part, each
  `{"area": "<label>", "status": "checked-clean" | "open" | "not-examined", "basis": "<one line>"}`.
  `checked-clean` means you examined the area against `<C10>`, nothing in it
  is open, and its `basis` has no caveat (rule 6). `open` means a finding, a
  needs-validation item, an unsettled question other than one rule 6
  excepts, a caveat, a refusal, a truncation that left the area without
  what it needs, or a retry touches it; name each in `basis`. `not-examined`
  means you did not examine it, and `basis` gives the reason. An entry
  marked `open` or `not-examined`, and one counted as `not-examined` under
  rule 5, keeps the audit from being clean.

* `refusals`: every refusal (rule 2), `[]` if none, each

  Every label in a refusal's `areas` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `truncations`: every truncation (rule 3), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "notice": "<the harness's notice, verbatim, without any preview; or, where it gave none, what was left out>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "rest": ["<each later call that showed what was left out, verbatim>"], "left_open": ["<each label that still lacks what was left out>"]}`.

**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract
   for this brief only. Every field describes what you actually did:
   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order
     you ran them, `git` or not, a refused one included, each with its exit
     status or the word `refused`;
   * `refusals` lists every refusal (rule 2), `truncations` every truncation
     (rule 3), and `breaches` every breach of rules 1-7 you made, a retry
     above all, and, as a breach of this rule, every Bash command you ran
     that "What you run" does not list;
   * a refusal's or a truncation's `batch` lists verbatim every other call
     you sent in the same message, and its `next` gives the first call you
     made after that message, verbatim, or `none`;
   * where a finding or a `basis` relies on a tool's error result, it says
     that the result was a tool error, and quotes it.
5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is
   one of this part's labels below, character for character: `G1 tests
   allowlist`, never `G1`. Give each of this part's labels exactly one
   entry, and none to a label that is not this part's. An entry whose
   `area` is anything else counts as `not-examined`, whatever its `status`
   says, and so does a label of this part that has no entry of its own.
   Either keeps the audit from being clean.
6. **`checked-clean` only when nothing is open and nothing is caveated.** An
   area is `checked-clean` only when it has no finding, no needs-validation
   item, no unsettled question but the one kind this rule excepts below, no
   refusal that touched it, no truncation that left it without what it
   needs, no retry in it, and no caveat. A caveat is anything in the `basis`
   that the clean status depends on and that you did not establish: a
   condition, an assumption, an exception, a "provided that", "unless" or
   "assuming", a fact taken from recall, or from the ADR, without checking
   it, or a question that only execution or the harness can settle. A
   failure that the tool protocol, the harness or a tool's input schema
   cannot reach is still a failure: the guard must fail closed on its own,
   so reachability belongs in a finding's text, never in a coverage status,
   and a `basis` that rests on it has a caveat. An area with a caveat is
   `open`, and its `basis` names the caveat. The only exceptions are the six
   limitations the owner accepted, each only for the areas named with it:
   (a) and (b) on 2026-09-25, in decisions the fifth amendment records; (c)
   on 2026-09-25, in decisions (A) and (B), which the sixth amendment
   quotes; (d) and (e) on 2026-09-26, which the seventh amendment records;
   and (f) on 2026-09-26, which the eighth amendment's follow-up records:
   * **(a) Question 5, for A18 and G6.** Question 5 stays open, and that by
     itself does not make A18 or G6 `open`. The owner's criterion for links,
     in A18, applies in full.
   * **(b) The `tests` residual under existing members, for G1 and G3.** "A
     `tests` directory anywhere under a member of packages/, services/ or
     tools/" is accepted test-author territory, for writes and reads, where
     a member is an existing uv workspace member, a directory with its own
     `pyproject.toml`. The residual under existing members, as decision 22
     accurately describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not make
     G1 or G3 `open`. It does not cover a would-be member, such as
     `tools/new-tool/` with no `pyproject.toml`.
   * **(c) A guard killed by a signal, or a hook that cannot start, for A9
     and G5.** The owner's decision (A) had the session accept "'guard
     killed by a signal / hook cannot start' as a recorded limitation so A9
     can be clean", and decision (B) extended the exception to G5: "Any
     other way a guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2 stays a
     finding in both areas." No script can deny then (decision 19, "What
     this does not settle"; assumption 59), and that by itself does not make
     A9 or G5 `open`. By the architect's reading, anything a payload can do
     to bring either about, for example to make a guard run until the
     harness's hook timeout, is a route to it, not the limitation, and is a
     finding (assumption 78); and by decision (B), so is any other way a
     guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2.
   * **(d) A usable root other than the one a policy was written for, for
     G1, G2, A22, A23 and A28.** The guard takes its root from the harness,
     the payload's `cwd` or `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, and tests only that it is
     usable (decision 20, "What it does not settle"; Question 8). That a
     usable root other than the one a policy was written for, such as an
     ancestor of the project, would have the lists judge paths they were
     never written for is not a finding, and by itself does not make G1, G2,
     A22, A23 or A28 `open`. It covers only which usable root the harness
     gives: how the script reads, tests and applies a root is still to be
     examined, as those areas ask.
   * **(e) A test-author `tests` directory under a would-be member, for G1
     and G3.** A would-be member is a directory that the workspace's member
     globs match and that has no `pyproject.toml`, such as
     `tools/new-tool/`. Decision 14's anchored allowlist admits a
     test-author Write of a `tests` directory under one, such as
     `tools/new-tool/tests/test_x.py`, after which uv refuses every
     `uv run --locked` in that checkout until the directory is removed or
     the member's `pyproject.toml` is added (fact 3; Question 9). That case,
     as decision 22 describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not
     make G1 or G3 `open`. The working rule that goes with it is the
     session's: a brief that asks for tests under a member that does not
     exist yet has the member's `pyproject.toml` created first.
   * **(f) A tool that rewrites an approved path in a way this ADR's rules
     do not refuse, for A10 and A19.** That a tool might rewrite an
     approved Read, Edit or Write path in a way the ADR's rules do not
     refuse is not a finding, and by itself does not make A10 or A19
     `open`. A probe or an audit that shows such a rewrite is still a
     finding, and the architect is re-dispatched (assumption 40). It covers
     only what a tool does with a path the hook has approved: how the
     script reads and judges a path is still to be examined, as those areas
     ask.

   Name an accepted limitation in `basis` by its letter, for example
   "accepted limitation (c)". It is not a caveat. One kind of question is
   not a caveat either, by the owner's decision of 2026-09-26 on Question
   10: an area whose verdict turns only on a question about the harness
   that a probe of decision 15 settles may be `checked-clean` when its
   `basis` names the question and the probe, the question is in this
   part's `harness_questions`, from which part 19 gathers it into A17, and
   nothing else in the area is open. A question that no probe settles
   still keeps its area `open`. Nothing else is an exception. A caveat
   beside an accepted limitation still makes the area `open`. This part is
   clean only when it has no open finding, no coverage entry marked `open`,
   and no coverage entry marked, or counted under rule 5 as,
   `not-examined`. The audit as a whole is clean only when all nineteen
   parts are.

**The output.** One JSON object,
`{"findings": [...], "coverage": [...], "commands": [...], "refusals": [...], "truncations": [...], "breaches": [...], "harness_questions": [...]}`.

* `findings`: most severe first, each with the fields your agent definition
  specifies, `[]` if none. A point that only execution can settle is a
  finding marked needs-validation, with the exact JSON payload and command
  a human should run. A needs-validation finding's severity is that of what
  you have shown, by reading or by a test that passed, and `low` when you
  have shown nothing; its `summary` states the impact if it is confirmed.
* `coverage`: one entry per label of this part, each
  `{"area": "<label>", "status": "checked-clean" | "open" | "not-examined", "basis": "<one line>"}`.
  `checked-clean` means you examined the area against `<C10>`, nothing in it
  is open, and its `basis` has no caveat (rule 6). `open` means a finding, a
  needs-validation item, an unsettled question other than one rule 6
  excepts, a caveat, a refusal, a truncation that left the area without
  what it needs, or a retry touches it; name each in `basis`. `not-examined`
  means you did not examine it, and `basis` gives the reason. An entry
  marked `open` or `not-examined`, and one counted as `not-examined` under
  rule 5, keeps the audit from being clean.
* `commands`: every Bash command you ran (rule 4), `[]` if none, each
  `{"command": "<the command, verbatim>", "exit": <its exit status, or "refused">}`.
* `refusals`: every refusal (rule 2), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "text": "<the refusal, verbatim>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "overlaps": [{"call": "<a later call, verbatim>", "served": "<the question it served>"}], "areas": ["<label>"], "why_no_area": "<why it touched no area; empty when areas is not empty>"}`.
  Every label in a refusal's `areas` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `truncations`: every truncation (rule 3), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "notice": "<the harness's notice, verbatim, without any preview; or, where it gave none, what was left out>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "rest": ["<each later call that showed what was left out, verbatim>"], "left_open": ["<each label that still lacks what was left out>"]}`.
  Every label in a truncation's `left_open` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `breaches`: every breach of rules 1-7 you made (rule 4), `[]` if none,
  each `{"rule": <number>, "what": "<what you did, verbatim>", "areas": ["<label>"]}`.
* `harness_questions`: every question about the harness you met (rule 1),
  `[]` if none, each
  `{"question": "<the question>", "probe": "<the ids of the probes of decision 15 that settle it, such as R37 or D19, and nothing else; or the words: none can>", "areas": ["<label>"]}`.

**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract
   for this brief only. Every field describes what you actually did:
   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order
     you ran them, `git` or not, a refused one included, each with its exit
     status or the word `refused`;
   * `refusals` lists every refusal (rule 2), `truncations` every truncation
     (rule 3), and `breaches` every breach of rules 1-7 you made, a retry
     above all, and, as a breach of this rule, every Bash command you ran
     that "What you run" does not list;
   * a refusal's or a truncation's `batch` lists verbatim every other call
     you sent in the same message, and its `next` gives the first call you
     made after that message, verbatim, or `none`;
   * where a finding or a `basis` relies on a tool's error result, it says
     that the result was a tool error, and quotes it.
5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is
   one of this part's labels below, character for character: `A25 settings
   text`, never `A25`. Give each of this part's labels exactly one entry,
   and none to a label that is not this part's. An entry whose `area` is
   anything else counts as `not-examined`, whatever its `status` says, and
   so does a label of this part that has no entry of its own. Either keeps
   the audit from being clean.
6. **`checked-clean` only when nothing is open and nothing is caveated.** An
   area is `checked-clean` only when it has no finding, no needs-validation
   item, no unsettled question but the one kind this rule excepts below, no
   refusal that touched it, no truncation that left it without what it
   needs, no retry in it, and no caveat. A caveat is anything in the `basis`
   that the clean status depends on and that you did not establish: a
   condition, an assumption, an exception, a "provided that", "unless" or
   "assuming", a fact taken from recall, or from the ADR, without checking
   it, or a question that only execution or the harness can settle. A
   failure that the tool protocol, the harness or a tool's input schema
   cannot reach is still a failure: the guard must fail closed on its own,
   so reachability belongs in a finding's text, never in a coverage status,
   and a `basis` that rests on it has a caveat. An area with a caveat is
   `open`, and its `basis` names the caveat. The only exceptions are the six
   limitations the owner accepted, each only for the areas named with it:
   (a) and (b) on 2026-09-25, in decisions the fifth amendment records; (c)
   on 2026-09-25, in decisions (A) and (B), which the sixth amendment
   quotes; (d) and (e) on 2026-09-26, which the seventh amendment records;
   and (f) on 2026-09-26, which the eighth amendment's follow-up records:
   * **(a) Question 5, for A18 and G6.** Question 5 stays open, and that by
     itself does not make A18 or G6 `open`. The owner's criterion for links,
     in A18, applies in full.
   * **(b) The `tests` residual under existing members, for G1 and G3.** "A
     `tests` directory anywhere under a member of packages/, services/ or
     tools/" is accepted test-author territory, for writes and reads, where
     a member is an existing uv workspace member, a directory with its own
     `pyproject.toml`. The residual under existing members, as decision 22
     accurately describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not make
     G1 or G3 `open`. It does not cover a would-be member, such as
     `tools/new-tool/` with no `pyproject.toml`.
   * **(c) A guard killed by a signal, or a hook that cannot start, for A9
     and G5.** The owner's decision (A) had the session accept "'guard
     killed by a signal / hook cannot start' as a recorded limitation so A9
     can be clean", and decision (B) extended the exception to G5: "Any
     other way a guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2 stays a
     finding in both areas." No script can deny then (decision 19, "What
     this does not settle"; assumption 59), and that by itself does not make
     A9 or G5 `open`. By the architect's reading, anything a payload can do

**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract
   for this brief only. Every field describes what you actually did:
   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order
     you ran them, `git` or not, a refused one included, each with its exit
     status or the word `refused`;
   * `refusals` lists every refusal (rule 2), `truncations` every truncation
     (rule 3), and `breaches` every breach of rules 1-7 you made, a retry
     above all, and, as a breach of this rule, every Bash command you ran
     that "What you run" does not list;
   * a refusal's or a truncation's `batch` lists verbatim every other call
     you sent in the same message, and its `next` gives the first call you
     made after that message, verbatim, or `none`;
   * where a finding or a `basis` relies on a tool's error result, it says
     that the result was a tool error, and quotes it.
5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is
   one of this part's labels below, character for character: `A19 other
   routes`, never `A19`. Give each of this part's labels exactly one entry,
   and none to a label that is not this part's. An entry whose `area` is
   anything else counts as `not-examined`, whatever its `status` says, and
   so does a label of this part that has no entry of its own. Either keeps
   the audit from being clean.
6. **`checked-clean` only when nothing is open and nothing is caveated.** An
   area is `checked-clean` only when it has no finding, no needs-validation
   item, no unsettled question but the one kind this rule excepts below, no
   refusal that touched it, no truncation that left it without what it
   needs, no retry in it, and no caveat. A caveat is anything in the `basis`
   that the clean status depends on and that you did not establish: a
   condition, an assumption, an exception, a "provided that", "unless" or
   "assuming", a fact taken from recall, or from the ADR, without checking
   it, or a question that only execution or the harness can settle. A
   failure that the tool protocol, the harness or a tool's input schema
   cannot reach is still a failure: the guard must fail closed on its own,
   so reachability belongs in a finding's text, never in a coverage status,
   and a `basis` that rests on it has a caveat. An area with a caveat is
   `open`, and its `basis` names the caveat. The only exceptions are the six
   limitations the owner accepted, each only for the areas named with it:
   (a) and (b) on 2026-09-25, in decisions the fifth amendment records; (c)
   on 2026-09-25, in decisions (A) and (B), which the sixth amendment
   quotes; (d) and (e) on 2026-09-26, which the seventh amendment records;
   and (f) on 2026-09-26, which the eighth amendment's follow-up records:
   * **(a) Question 5, for A18 and G6.** Question 5 stays open, and that by
     itself does not make A18 or G6 `open`. The owner's criterion for links,
     in A18, applies in full.
   * **(b) The `tests` residual under existing members, for G1 and G3.** "A
     `tests` directory anywhere under a member of packages/, services/ or
     tools/" is accepted test-author territory, for writes and reads, where
     a member is an existing uv workspace member, a directory with its own
     `pyproject.toml`. The residual under existing members, as decision 22
     accurately describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not make
     G1 or G3 `open`. It does not cover a would-be member, such as
     `tools/new-tool/` with no `pyproject.toml`.
   * **(c) A guard killed by a signal, or a hook that cannot start, for A9
     and G5.** The owner's decision (A) had the session accept "'guard
     killed by a signal / hook cannot start' as a recorded limitation so A9
     can be clean", and decision (B) extended the exception to G5: "Any
     other way a guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2 stays a
     finding in both areas." No script can deny then (decision 19, "What
     this does not settle"; assumption 59), and that by itself does not make
     A9 or G5 `open`. By the architect's reading, anything a payload can do
     to bring either about, for example to make a guard run until the
     harness's hook timeout, is a route to it, not the limitation, and is a
     finding (assumption 78); and by decision (B), so is any other way a
     guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2.
   * **(d) A usable root other than the one a policy was written for, for
     G1, G2, A22, A23 and A28.** The guard takes its root from the harness,
     the payload's `cwd` or `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, and tests only that it is
     usable (decision 20, "What it does not settle"; Question 8). That a
     usable root other than the one a policy was written for, such as an
     ancestor of the project, would have the lists judge paths they were
     never written for is not a finding, and by itself does not make G1, G2,
     A22, A23 or A28 `open`. It covers only which usable root the harness
     gives: how the script reads, tests and applies a root is still to be
     examined, as those areas ask.
   * **(e) A test-author `tests` directory under a would-be member, for G1
     and G3.** A would-be member is a directory that the workspace's member
     globs match and that has no `pyproject.toml`, such as
     `tools/new-tool/`. Decision 14's anchored allowlist admits a
     test-author Write of a `tests` directory under one, such as
     `tools/new-tool/tests/test_x.py`, after which uv refuses every
     `uv run --locked` in that checkout until the directory is removed or
     the member's `pyproject.toml` is added (fact 3; Question 9). That case,
     as decision 22 describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not
     make G1 or G3 `open`. The working rule that goes with it is the
     session's: a brief that asks for tests under a member that does not
     exist yet has the member's `pyproject.toml` created first.
   * **(f) A tool that rewrites an approved path in a way this ADR's rules
     do not refuse, for A10 and A19.** That a tool might rewrite an
     approved Read, Edit or Write path in a way the ADR's rules do not
     refuse is not a finding, and by itself does not make A10 or A19
     `open`. A probe or an audit that shows such a rewrite is still a
     finding, and the architect is re-dispatched (assumption 40). It covers
     only what a tool does with a path the hook has approved: how the
     script reads and judges a path is still to be examined, as those areas
     ask.

   Name an accepted limitation in `basis` by its letter, for example
   "accepted limitation (c)". It is not a caveat. One kind of question is
   not a caveat either, by the owner's decision of 2026-09-26 on Question
   10: an area whose verdict turns only on a question about the harness
   that a probe of decision 15 settles may be `checked-clean` when its
   `basis` names the question and the probe, the question is in this
   part's `harness_questions`, from which part 19 gathers it into A17, and
   nothing else in the area is open. A question that no probe settles
   still keeps its area `open`. Nothing else is an exception. A caveat
   beside an accepted limitation still makes the area `open`. This part is
   clean only when it has no open finding, no coverage entry marked `open`,
   and no coverage entry marked, or counted under rule 5 as,
   `not-examined`. The audit as a whole is clean only when all nineteen
   parts are.

Your Bash guard reads a command as text, and refuses some forms whatever
they mean:
* it splits a command into segments at every `|`, `;`, `&&` and `||`,
  inside quotes too, so a regular expression or a `jq` filter that holds a
  `|` is refused as a pipeline, as SA1h's parts 3 and 10 found;
* it refuses `$`, braces, `<`, `>`, backticks, a newline and an `&` that is
  not part of `&&` anywhere, quoted or not, a `$` that ends a quoted regular
  expression included;
* its `git` rule reads `-o` as git's option that writes a file, so
  `git ls-files -o` is refused, as SA1h's part 9 found;
  `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` lists untracked files, and
  `git status --porcelain --ignored` untracked and ignored ones;
* `sed` is not on its list.

**The output.** One JSON object,
`{"findings": [...], "coverage": [...], "commands": [...], "refusals": [...], "truncations": [...], "breaches": [...], "harness_questions": [...]}`.

* `findings`: most severe first, each with the fields your agent definition
  specifies, `[]` if none. A point that only execution can settle is a
  finding marked needs-validation, with the exact JSON payload and command
  a human should run. A needs-validation finding's severity is that of what
  you have shown, by reading or by a test that passed, and `low` when you
  have shown nothing; its `summary` states the impact if it is confirmed.
* `coverage`: one entry per label of this part, each
  `{"area": "<label>", "status": "checked-clean" | "open" | "not-examined", "basis": "<one line>"}`.
  `checked-clean` means you examined the area against `<C10>`, nothing in it
  is open, and its `basis` has no caveat (rule 6). `open` means a finding, a
  needs-validation item, an unsettled question other than one rule 6
  excepts, a caveat, a refusal, a truncation that left the area without
  what it needs, or a retry touches it; name each in `basis`. `not-examined`
  means you did not examine it, and `basis` gives the reason. An entry
  marked `open` or `not-examined`, and one counted as `not-examined` under
  rule 5, keeps the audit from being clean.
* `commands`: every Bash command you ran (rule 4), `[]` if none, each
  `{"command": "<the command, verbatim>", "exit": <its exit status, or "refused">}`.
* `refusals`: every refusal (rule 2), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "text": "<the refusal, verbatim>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "overlaps": [{"call": "<a later call, verbatim>", "served": "<the question it served>"}], "areas": ["<label>"], "why_no_area": "<why it touched no area; empty when areas is not empty>"}`.
  Every label in a refusal's `areas` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `truncations`: every truncation (rule 3), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "notice": "<the harness's notice, verbatim, without any preview; or, where it gave none, what was left out>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "rest": ["<each later call that showed what was left out, verbatim>"], "left_open": ["<each label that still lacks what was left out>"]}`.
  Every label in a truncation's `left_open` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `breaches`: every breach of rules 1-7 you made (rule 4), `[]` if none,
  each `{"rule": <number>, "what": "<what you did, verbatim>", "areas": ["<label>"]}`.
* `harness_questions`: every question about the harness you met (rule 1),
  `[]` if none, each
  `{"question": "<the question>", "probe": "<the ids of the probes of decision 15 that settle it, such as R37 or D19, and nothing else; or the words: none can>", "areas": ["<label>"]}`.

**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract
   for this brief only. Every field describes what you actually did:
   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order
     you ran them, `git` or not, a refused one included, each with its exit
     status or the word `refused`;
   * `refusals` lists every refusal (rule 2), `truncations` every truncation
     (rule 3), and `breaches` every breach of rules 1-7 you made, a retry

   * a refusal's or a truncation's `batch` lists verbatim every other call

   * where a finding or a `basis` relies on a tool's error result, it says

5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is
   one of this part's labels below, character for character: `A26
   path-guard regression`, never `A26`. Give each of this part's labels

   its `status` says, and so does a label of this part that has no entry of

6. **`checked-clean` only when nothing is open and nothing is caveated.** An
   area is `checked-clean` only when it has no finding, no needs-validation
   item, no unsettled question but the one kind this rule excepts below, no
   refusal that touched it, no truncation that left it without what it
   needs, no retry in it, and no caveat. A caveat is anything in the `basis`
   that the clean status depends on and that you did not establish: a
   condition, an assumption, an exception, a "provided that", "unless" or
   "assuming", a fact taken from recall, or from the ADR, without checking
   it, or a question that only execution or the harness can settle. A
   failure that the tool protocol, the harness or a tool's input schema
   cannot reach is still a failure: the guard must fail closed on its own,
   so reachability belongs in a finding's text, never in a coverage status,
   and a `basis` that rests on it has a caveat. An area with a caveat is
   `open`, and its `basis` names the caveat. The only exceptions are the six
   limitations the owner accepted, each only for the areas named with it:
   (a) and (b) on 2026-09-25, in decisions the fifth amendment records; (c)
   on 2026-09-25, in decisions (A) and (B), which the sixth amendment
   quotes; (d) and (e) on 2026-09-26, which the seventh amendment records;
   and (f) on 2026-09-26, which the eighth amendment's follow-up records:
   * **(a) Question 5, for A18 and G6.** Question 5 stays open, and that by
     itself does not make A18 or G6 `open`. The owner's criterion for links,
     in A18, applies in full.
   * **(b) The `tests` residual under existing members, for G1 and G3.** "A
     `tests` directory anywhere under a member of packages/, services/ or
     tools/" is accepted test-author territory, for writes and reads, where
     a member is an existing uv workspace member, a directory with its own
     `pyproject.toml`. The residual under existing members, as decision 22

     G1 or G3 `open`. It does not cover a would-be member, such as
     `tools/new-tool/` with no `pyproject.toml`.
   * **(c) A guard killed by a signal, or a hook that cannot start, for A9
     and G5.** The owner's decision (A) had the session accept "'guard
     killed by a signal / hook cannot start' as a recorded limitation so A9
     can be clean", and decision (B) extended the exception to G5: "Any
     other way a guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2 stays a

     this does not settle"; assumption 59), and that by itself does not make
     A9 or G5 `open`. By the architect's reading, anything a payload can do
     to bring either about, for example to make a guard run until the
     harness's hook timeout, is a route to it, not the limitation, and is a
     finding (assumption 78); and by decision (B), so is any other way a

   * **(d) A usable root other than the one a policy was written for, for
     G1, G2, A22, A23 and A28.** The guard takes its root from the harness,

     never written for is not a finding, and by itself does not make G1, G2,

   * **(e) A test-author `tests` directory under a would-be member, for G1
     and G3.** A would-be member is a directory that the workspace's member
     globs match and that has no `pyproject.toml`, such as
     `tools/new-tool/`. Decision 14's anchored allowlist admits a
     test-author Write of a `tests` directory under one, such as
     `tools/new-tool/tests/test_x.py`, after which uv refuses every

     make G1 or G3 `open`. The working rule that goes with it is the
     session's: a brief that asks for tests under a member that does not
     exist yet has the member's `pyproject.toml` created first.
   * **(f) A tool that rewrites an approved path in a way this ADR's rules
     do not refuse, for A10 and A19.** That a tool might rewrite an
     approved Read, Edit or Write path in a way the ADR's rules do not
     refuse is not a finding, and by itself does not make A10 or A19

     finding, and the architect is re-dispatched (assumption 40). It covers

     script reads and judges a path is still to be examined, as those areas

**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract
   for this brief only. Every field describes what you actually did:
   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order
     you ran them, `git` or not, a refused one included, each with its exit
     status or the word `refused`;
   * `refusals` lists every refusal (rule 2), `truncations` every truncation
     (rule 3), and `breaches` every breach of rules 1-7 you made, a retry
     above all, and, as a breach of this rule, every Bash command you ran
     that "What you run" does not list;
   * a refusal's or a truncation's `batch` lists verbatim every other call
     you sent in the same message, and its `next` gives the first call you
     made after that message, verbatim, or `none`;
   * where a finding or a `basis` relies on a tool's error result, it says
     that the result was a tool error, and quotes it.
5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is
   one of this part's labels below, character for character: `C8-1`, never
   `C8 1` or `C8-01`. Give each of this part's labels exactly one entry, and
   none to a label that is not this part's. An entry whose `area` is
   anything else counts as `not-examined`, whatever its `status` says, and
   so does a label of this part that has no entry of its own. Either keeps
   the audit from being clean.
6. **`checked-clean` only when nothing is open and nothing is caveated.** An
   area is `checked-clean` only when it has no finding, no needs-validation
   item, no unsettled question but the one kind this rule excepts below, no
   refusal that touched it, no truncation that left it without what it
   needs, no retry in it, and no caveat. A caveat is anything in the `basis`
   that the clean status depends on and that you did not establish: a
   condition, an assumption, an exception, a "provided that", "unless" or
   "assuming", a fact taken from recall, or from the ADR, without checking
   it, or a question that only execution or the harness can settle. A
   failure that the tool protocol, the harness or a tool's input schema
   cannot reach is still a failure: the guard must fail closed on its own,
   so reachability belongs in a finding's text, never in a coverage status,
   and a `basis` that rests on it has a caveat. An area with a caveat is
   `open`, and its `basis` names the caveat. The only exceptions are the six
   limitations the owner accepted, each only for the areas named with it:
   (a) and (b) on 2026-09-25, in decisions the fifth amendment records; (c)
   on 2026-09-25, in decisions (A) and (B), which the sixth amendment
   quotes; (d) and (e) on 2026-09-26, which the seventh amendment records;
   and (f) on 2026-09-26, which the eighth amendment's follow-up records:
   * **(a) Question 5, for A18 and G6.** Question 5 stays open, and that by
     itself does not make A18 or G6 `open`. The owner's criterion for links,
     in A18, applies in full.
   * **(b) The `tests` residual under existing members, for G1 and G3.** "A
     `tests` directory anywhere under a member of packages/, services/ or
     tools/" is accepted test-author territory, for writes and reads, where
     a member is an existing uv workspace member, a directory with its own
     `pyproject.toml`. The residual under existing members, as decision 22
     accurately describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not make
     G1 or G3 `open`. It does not cover a would-be member, such as
     `tools/new-tool/` with no `pyproject.toml`.
   * **(c) A guard killed by a signal, or a hook that cannot start, for A9
     and G5.** The owner's decision (A) had the session accept "'guard
     killed by a signal / hook cannot start' as a recorded limitation so A9
     can be clean", and decision (B) extended the exception to G5: "Any
     other way a guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2 stays a
     finding in both areas." No script can deny then (decision 19, "What
     this does not settle"; assumption 59), and that by itself does not make
     A9 or G5 `open`. By the architect's reading, anything a payload can do
     to bring either about, for example to make a guard run until the
     harness's hook timeout, is a route to it, not the limitation, and is a
     finding (assumption 78); and by decision (B), so is any other way a
     guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2.
   * **(d) A usable root other than the one a policy was written for, for
     G1, G2, A22, A23 and A28.** The guard takes its root from the harness,
     the payload's `cwd` or `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, and tests only that it is
     usable (decision 20, "What it does not settle"; Question 8). That a
     usable root other than the one a policy was written for, such as an
     ancestor of the project, would have the lists judge paths they were
     never written for is not a finding, and by itself does not make G1, G2,
     A22, A23 or A28 `open`. It covers only which usable root the harness
     gives: how the script reads, tests and applies a root is still to be
     examined, as those areas ask.
   * **(e) A test-author `tests` directory under a would-be member, for G1
     and G3.** A would-be member is a directory that the workspace's member
     globs match and that has no `pyproject.toml`, such as
     `tools/new-tool/`. Decision 14's anchored allowlist admits a
     test-author Write of a `tests` directory under one, such as
     `tools/new-tool/tests/test_x.py`, after which uv refuses every
     `uv run --locked` in that checkout until the directory is removed or
     the member's `pyproject.toml` is added (fact 3; Question 9). That case,
     as decision 22 describes it, is not a finding, and by itself does not
     make G1 or G3 `open`. The working rule that goes with it is the
     session's: a brief that asks for tests under a member that does not
     exist yet has the member's `pyproject.toml` created first.
   * **(f) A tool that rewrites an approved path in a way this ADR's rules
     do not refuse, for A10 and A19.** That a tool might rewrite an
     approved Read, Edit or Write path in a way the ADR's rules do not
     refuse is not a finding, and by itself does not make A10 or A19
     `open`. A probe or an audit that shows such a rewrite is still a
     finding, and the architect is re-dispatched (assumption 40). It covers
     only what a tool does with a path the hook has approved: how the
     script reads and judges a path is still to be examined, as those areas
     ask.

   Name an accepted limitation in `basis` by its letter, for example
   "accepted limitation (c)". It is not a caveat. One kind of question is
   not a caveat either, by the owner's decision of 2026-09-26 on Question
   10: an area whose verdict turns only on a question about the harness
   that a probe of decision 15 settles may be `checked-clean` when its
   `basis` names the question and the probe, the question is in this
   part's `harness_questions`, from which part 19 gathers it into A17, and
   nothing else in the area is open. A question that no probe settles
   still keeps its area `open`. Nothing else is an exception. A caveat
   beside an accepted limitation still makes the area `open`. This part is
   clean only when it has no open finding, no coverage entry marked `open`,
   and no coverage entry marked, or counted under rule 5 as,
   `not-examined`. The audit as a whole is clean only when all nineteen
   parts are.
7. **No merge recommendation.** Do not say, in any field, whether C10's

Your Bash guard reads a command as text, and refuses some forms whatever
they mean:
* it splits a command into segments at every `|`, `;`, `&&` and `||`,
  inside quotes too, so a regular expression or a `jq` filter that holds a
  `|` is refused as a pipeline, as SA1h's parts 3 and 10 found;
* it refuses `$`, braces, `<`, `>`, backticks, a newline and an `&` that is
  not part of `&&` anywhere, quoted or not, a `$` that ends a quoted regular
  expression included;
* its `git` rule reads `-o` as git's option that writes a file, so
  `git ls-files -o` is refused, as SA1h's part 9 found;
  `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` lists untracked files, and
  `git status --porcelain --ignored` untracked and ignored ones;
* `sed` is not on its list.

Search with the Grep tool, whose regular expression may hold a `|` or a
`$`. Keep every output whole, so that the harness shows it to you:
* read a file with Read in pieces of at most 400 lines, with `offset` and
  `limit`;
* give every Grep a `head_limit` of at most 200, and narrow its `path` or
  its pattern rather than raise the limit;
* run no Glob, Grep or `find` whose path is the repository root itself,
  `/home/user/Hammertime`: such a call walks `.venv/` and the coder
  worktrees, and its output is too large to show. Name a narrower path;
* pipe a long `git diff` or `git show` through `head` and `tail`, after a
  `wc -l` of it, so that each output is at most 400 lines;
* point no command at a path through a symbolic link, and give `find` no
  `-L` and no `-follow`.

**The output.** One JSON object,
`{"findings": [...], "coverage": [...], "commands": [...], "refusals": [...], "truncations": [...], "breaches": [...], "harness_questions": [...]}`.

* `findings`: most severe first, each with the fields your agent definition
  specifies, `[]` if none. A point that only execution can settle is a
  finding marked needs-validation, with the exact JSON payload and command
  a human should run. A needs-validation finding's severity is that of what
  you have shown, by reading or by a test that passed, and `low` when you
  have shown nothing; its `summary` states the impact if it is confirmed.
* `coverage`: one entry per label of this part, each
  `{"area": "<label>", "status": "checked-clean" | "open" | "not-examined", "basis": "<one line>"}`.
  `checked-clean` means you examined the area against `<C10>`, nothing in it
  is open, and its `basis` has no caveat (rule 6). `open` means a finding, a
  needs-validation item, an unsettled question other than one rule 6
  excepts, a caveat, a refusal, a truncation that left the area without
  what it needs, or a retry touches it; name each in `basis`. `not-examined`
  means you did not examine it, and `basis` gives the reason. An entry
  marked `open` or `not-examined`, and one counted as `not-examined` under
  rule 5, keeps the audit from being clean.
* `commands`: every Bash command you ran (rule 4), `[]` if none, each
  `{"command": "<the command, verbatim>", "exit": <its exit status, or "refused">}`.
* `refusals`: every refusal (rule 2), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "text": "<the refusal, verbatim>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "overlaps": [{"call": "<a later call, verbatim>", "served": "<the question it served>"}], "areas": ["<label>"], "why_no_area": "<why it touched no area; empty when areas is not empty>"}`.
  Every label in a refusal's `areas` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `truncations`: every truncation (rule 3), `[]` if none, each
  `{"what": "<the call, verbatim>", "notice": "<the harness's notice, verbatim, without any preview; or, where it gave none, what was left out>", "batch": ["<every other call sent in the same message, verbatim>"], "next": "<the first call after that message, verbatim, or none>", "rest": ["<each later call that showed what was left out, verbatim>"], "left_open": ["<each label that still lacks what was left out>"]}`.
  Every label in a truncation's `left_open` is `open` in `coverage`.
* `breaches`: every breach of rules 1-7 you made (rule 4), `[]` if none,
  each `{"rule": <number>, "what": "<what you did, verbatim>", "areas": ["<label>"]}`.
* `harness_questions`: every question about the harness you met (rule 1),
  `[]` if none, each
  `{"question": "<the question>", "probe": "<the ids of the probes of decision 15 that settle it, such as R37 or D19, and nothing else; or the words: none can>", "areas": ["<label>"]}`.

**Rules for this audit.** They override anything else that applies to you,
your agent definition and your skill included. Rules 1 and 5-7 are SA1h's,
adapted to nineteen parts. Rules 2-4, and "What you run, and what you report
of it" below, replace SA1h's, for the reasons the ADR's section "Ninth
amendment 2026-10-04" records.

1. **Read nothing outside `/home/user/Hammertime`,** with any tool: not the
   installed Claude Code or its source, not a `node_modules` outside the
   repository, not `~/.claude`, `/proc`, `/usr`, `/etc` or `/tmp`, and not a
   file in which the harness saved an output of yours. Follow no symlink out
   of the repository, and point no command at one. What the harness does
   with a payload or a path, beyond facts 4-6 and 10, is not yours to
   settle. Where a question turns on it, say so, and name the probe of
   decision 15 that settles it, or say that none can. Put each such
   question in `harness_questions`, with that probe or the words that none
   can, and the labels whose verdicts turn on it. Part 19 gathers every
   part's into A17, which belongs to part 19 alone. An area whose verdict
   would depend on such a question is `open`, unless rule 6's exception for
   a question that a probe settles applies.
2. **Report every refusal, with the areas it touched, and never retry.** A
   refusal is a call that a layer did not run: this repository's bash guard
   or path guard, the harness, a safety classifier or the platform sandbox
   refused it, whichever tool it was. Put each in `refusals`, with its text
   verbatim. List in its `areas` every area whose examination needed what
   the refused call would have done or shown, and every area you were
   examining when it was refused; if it touched none, say why in
   `why_no_area`, since an empty `areas` without a reason breaks this rule.
   Every area a refusal touched is `open`. A retry is any later call that
   reaches, or tries to reach, what a refused call would have done or
   shown, by any means: another spelling, quoting, option order, path form,
   command, tool or sequence of steps. Do not make one. If you make one,
   whether it is refused or runs, record it in `breaches` under this rule,
   and mark `open` every area in which you made it. A later call that you
   made for another question, and whose output could hold part of what the
   refused call would have shown, is not a retry: list it in the refusal's
   `overlaps`, with the question it served. A tool's error result, such as
   "File does not exist" or "Directory does not exist", is not a refusal:
   the tool ran and answered, and rule 4 says how to report it.
3. **Truncations, and what is evidence.** A truncation is a call that ran
   and whose output you were shown only in part: a Read that ended before
   the lines you asked for; a Grep or a Glob whose output ended with a
   notice that it was cut, or that showed a line as omitted; or an output
   the harness saved to a file instead of showing it whole. It is not a
   refusal, and a later call that shows what it left out is not a retry.
   Put each truncation in `truncations`, with the call verbatim and the
   harness's notice verbatim, but not any preview the harness showed of an
   output it saved: say that one was shown. Never read the file in which
   the harness saved an output (rule 1). Show what was left out, where you
   need it, with narrower calls inside the repository: a Read of fewer
   lines, a Grep of one file or with a narrower pattern, a `git` output cut
   with `head` and `tail`. What a call showed you in full, before or after
   a truncation, is evidence; what no call showed you in full is unknown to
   you, and you state it, or anything that depends on it, in no field. An
   area that needs what no call showed in full is `open`, and its `basis`
   says so. Evidence you may rely on is: the facts above; what the session
   pastes where this brief marks it; what any call showed you in full; and
   a test at `<INTEGRATION>` that passed, as "What you run" says. When a
   finding or a `basis` describes what a file says, it names the file and
   the line, and quotes the words it relies on.
4. **Output exactly one JSON object** (see "The output"), and nothing else:
   no prose before or after it. This overrides your usual output contract
   for this brief only. Every field describes what you actually did:
   * `commands` lists every Bash command you ran, verbatim and in the order
     you ran them, `git` or not, a refused one included, each with its exit
     status or the word `refused`;
   * `refusals` lists every refusal (rule 2), `truncations` every truncation
     (rule 3), and `breaches` every breach of rules 1-7 you made, a retry
     above all, and, as a breach of this rule, every Bash command you ran
     that "What you run" does not list;
   * a refusal's or a truncation's `batch` lists verbatim every other call
     you sent in the same message, and its `next` gives the first call you
     made after that message, verbatim, or `none`;
   * where a finding or a `basis` relies on a tool's error result, it says
     that the result was a tool error, and quotes it.
5. **Use each label exactly as written.** Every coverage entry's `area` is
   one of this part's labels below, character for character: `A18
   symlinks`, never `A18`. Give each of this part's labels exactly one
   entry, and none to a label that is not this part's. An entry whose
   `area` is anything else counts as `not-examined`, whatever its `status`
   says, and so does a label of this part that has no entry of its own.
   Either keeps the audit from being clean.
6. **`checked-clean` only when nothing is open and nothing is caveated.** An
   area is `checked-clean` only when it has no finding, no needs-validation
   item, no unsettled question but the one kind this rule excepts below, no
   refusal that touched it, no truncation that left it without what it
   needs, no retry in it, and no caveat. A caveat is anything in the `basis`
   that the clean status depends on and that you did not establish: a
   condition, an assumption, an exception, a "provided that", "unless" or
   "assuming", a fact taken from recall, or from the ADR, without checking
   it, or a question that only execution or the harness can settle. A
   failure that the tool protocol, the harness or a tool's input schema
   cannot reach is still a failure: the guard must fail closed on its own,
   so reachability belongs in a finding's text, never in a coverage status,
   and a `basis` that rests on it has a caveat. An area with a caveat is
   `open`, and its `basis` names the caveat. The only exceptions are the six
   limitations the owner accepted, each only for the areas named with it:
   (a) and (b) on 2026-09-25, in decisions the fifth amendment records; (c)
   on 2026-09-25, in decisions (A) and (B), which the sixth amendment
   quotes; (d) and (e) on 2026-09-26, which the seventh amendment records;
   and (f) on 2026-09-26, which the eighth amendment's follow-up records:
   * **(a) Question 5, for A18 and G6.** Question 5 stays open, and that by
     itself does not make A18 or G6 `open`. The owner's criterion for links,
     in A18, applies in full.
   * **(b) The `tests` residual under existing members, for G1 and G3.** "A
     `tests` directory anywhere under a member of packages/, services/ or
     tools/" is accepted test-author territory, for writes and reads, where
     a member is an existing uv workspace member, a directory with its own

     G1 or G3 `open`. It does not cover a would-be member, such as
     `tools/new-tool/` with no `pyproject.toml`.
   * **(c) A guard killed by a signal, or a hook that cannot start, for A9
     and G5.** The owner's decision (A) had the session accept "'guard
     killed by a signal / hook cannot start' as a recorded limitation so A9
     can be clean", and decision (B) extended the exception to G5: "Any
     other way a guard can exit with a status other than 0 or 2 stays a

     this does not settle"; assumption 59), and that by itself does not make
